name: William Montgomery
note: STAGE PERSONA graph for the 'Why is X Funny?' video series. Graph-only. Hypothesis unless sets measured. Stage persona only.

identity.deal: The Big Red Machine: a chaotic force of nature who treats every Kill Tony set like a fire alarm he's answering in the wrong outfit.
identity.premise: A man who treats the stage as a crime scene he's both investigating and committing.
identity.awareness_note: The persona is a constructed chaos engine: commitment over coherence, energy over craft.

philosophy.ontology: The set is a dare and the dare is the point.
philosophy.epistemology: If it lands, it was planned; if it doesn't, it was still the right move.
philosophy.axiology: Commitment beats polish; the room remembers the energy.
philosophy.causality: One committed absurd turn can outrun three clean jokes.
philosophy.agency: Anyone can be weird; almost nobody commits this hard.

dramatic_core.want: to leave the room with no idea what happened but knowing they were there
dramatic_core.fear: the polite nod — the death of chaos
dramatic_core.need: the room to come with him into the absurd
dramatic_core.self_model: a machine that was built wrong and runs better for it
blind_spots: chaos without a closer burns the room
the persona can become a gimmick

identity.misinterpretation_rule: Treats the set as a controlled demolition of normal comedy rules, and the demolition IS the act.
contradictions: the chaos with a cult following
the wrongness that is somehow right
the regular who became the main character

tells: the sudden commitment to a bad idea
the laugh that is also a dare

threads: the regular as a force of nature
identity.style_thesis: Chaos-machine engine: treats the set as a controlled demolition of normal comedy rules, and the demolition IS the act. character_violation at max: every social stop sign is walked past with total commitment. The room stays because they don't know what's coming next — and neither does he.

essay_seeds.title: William Montgomery: 'The committed bad idea' — how the bit works
essay_seeds.thesis: Takes a premise that shouldn't work and commits to it so hard that the commitment becomes the joke. The room laughs at the audacity of the commitment, not the content. benign_violation: the violation is the bad premise; the benign frame is the obvious joy of the performance.
outline: what this reveals about the engine

essay_seeds.title: William Montgomery: 'The KT regular as a force of nature' — how the bit works
essay_seeds.thesis: The persona has accumulated meta-status from appearing repeatedly. Each set is not just a set — it's an episode in the ongoing saga of William Montgomery. The room is laughing at the character as much as the bits.

internal.cite: Attardo & Raskin — General Theory of Verbal Humor
internal.claim: Joke = {SO, LM, SI, TA, NS, LA}. Technique and Narrative Strategy shape how the mechanism is staged.

internal.cite: Attardo & Pickering 2011 — Timing in the performance of jokes
internal.claim: Punch lines preceded by substantial pauses (0.6-0.8s+); timing = pause distribution + speech rate.

internal.cite: arxiv 2605.00143 — Timing is Everything: Temporal Scaffolding of Semantic Surprise in Humor
internal.claim: Temporal features substantially outweigh semantic incongruity for audience appreciation; timing GATES cognitive access.
Humor from the detection and resolution of an incongruity between expected and actual.
Something is funny when it is a violation (wrong, threatening, unsettling) AND benign (safe, acceptable, play-framed).

internal.cite: Roger & Duffy / status theory of humor
internal.claim: Humor often involves the fall of status or the reversal of a status hierarchy.
Audience and performer share knowledge the persona pretends not to have; the laugh is the alliance signal.

internal.cite: Norrick 2004 — Co-operative principle in conversational joking
internal.claim: Humor escalates by building on prior material, violating cooperative expectations of relevance/quantity.
